title: Cornstarch for flour thickening a liquid as a slurry

exceptions.reason: The dish keeps cooking for a long time after it thickens (or it's frozen), and a cornstarch-thickened liquid thins again with long cooking and freezing.

evidence.basis: Knowledge packet 2026-10-13 item E1, PROPOSED (not approved). Research private/research/substitution-knowledge, cornstarch_for_flour_as_thickener (SOURCE_SUPPORTED): Argo SRC-FS-38#a (twice the thickening power: use half), Illinois Extension SRC-FS-34#a (2 tbsp flour or 1 tbsp cornstarch per cup of liquid), SRC-FS-32#a (2:1). Slurry only: a roux or fat-based sauce is a different technique (Illinois: flour works best there). Excluded by the step's own text: cooking 10 minutes or more after thickening, or freezing (Argo: avoid prolonged boiling; Argo, PSU: freezing). The 10-minute line and the 1/2 tbsp-1/2 cup input bounds are engineering choices.

ops.text: Stir the cornstarch into the cold liquid until smooth, then bring it to a full boil, stirring, and boil it for a minute; don't keep boiling it hard once it has thickened.

consequence.headline: Thicken it with half as much cornstarch instead of the flour.
consequence.reason: Cornstarch thickens about twice as much as flour, so half the amount by volume does the same job (Illinois Extension; Argo).
consequence.tradeoff: It turns glossy and see-through rather than opaque, and it thins again if it's boiled hard or long once thickened. Not kitchen-tested in this recipe.

proposal.text: Yes, with half as much cornstarch.
